result:
Before a city wakes, it belongs to small sounds. A delivery truck sighs at the curb. Someone unlocks a bakery. A broom whispers across pavement, pushing yesterday into a neat gray pile. Above it all, the windows hold their darkness a little longer, like people reluctant to leave warm beds.

I like imagining that every ordinary morning contains a thousand quiet acts of faith. Bread goes into ovens before anyone arrives hungry. Trains begin their routes before the platforms fill. A florist trims stems for celebrations not yet announced, apologies not yet spoken, tables still bare in empty dining rooms.

We often describe hope as something bright and dramatic, a flare against the night. But perhaps its usual form is practical. Perhaps hope wears an apron, checks the weather, charges a battery, and sets out an extra chair. It makes preparations for a future that has offered no firm guarantees.

This is not the same as believing everything will turn out well. Some bread burns. Some trains stop between stations. Some flowers remain unsold until their petals loosen. The world does not promise to reward our tenderness. Yet tenderness keeps appearing, stubborn as grass finding a seam in the sidewalk.

By noon, the city will seem made of schedules, transactions, noise. Its softer machinery will disappear beneath the obvious kind. Still, somewhere, someone will rinse a cup for another person. Someone will hold a door. And the day, without becoming perfect, will become a little more possible to live in.
